strengths: The 3D Field of Junctions is a genuinely non-trivial extension of the 2D FoJ prior [34]: the geometric formulation with intersecting planes, soft region indicators (Eq. 8), and smooth boundary fields (Eq. 9) requires substantive re-derivation for volumetric patches, and the paper is transparent about the added complexity (e.g., the 8-region vs. M=3-region discussion in Sec. 4.3).

As a training-free, explicit structural prior, the method directly addresses a well-motivated gap: data-driven 3D priors are impractical for full volumes, while untrained neural priors blur boundaries at low SNR. The no-hallucination property is a real advantage for medical/scientific imaging.

The formulation as a proximal-gradient regularizer (Sec. 4.5) is a useful generalization beyond the 2D FoJ, which required direct access to a noisy image; this makes the prior applicable to inverse problems such as tomography from indirect projections.

Experimental coverage is unusually broad for this type of paper: low-dose sparse-view CT (5 datasets, 3 noise levels, quantitative MS-SSIM and 3D PSNR), real cryo-ET data, and point cloud denoising under two noise models across 28 shapes, with consistently strong results against classical and neural baselines (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 6).

The ablation study (Tables 3 and 7) is thorough and includes runtime analysis; the finding that a single init/refine iteration suffices, and the patch-size/noise-level trend, are informative for practitioners.

The discussion honestly identifies limitations (no per-task hyperparameter tuning, computational cost), and multi-GPU/chunked implementation details suggest the method is practically usable; code release is promised.
weaknesses: The core idea is a direct transfer of the 2D FoJ prior [34] to 3D; while the engineering is substantial, the conceptual novelty is incremental. The paper's claims of 'engineering innovation' (Sec. 1) are somewhat vague, and high-level algorithmic novelty over plug-and-play piecewise-constant priors (e.g., TV, Mumford-Shah-type models) could be argued to be limited.

Missing comparisons against the untrained neural priors the paper criticizes: the introduction and related work argue that DIP, Deep Decoder, and INRs (WIRE, SIREN) denoise volumes but blur edges at low SNR, yet none of these appear as baselines in the CT or cryo-ET experiments. The claim of outperforming 'untrained neural' methods is thus not directly supported by evidence. BM4D, a standard 3D denoiser, is also absent.

No quantitative evidence is provided for the cryo-ET experiments (real data, no ground truth), so the strongest qualitative claims rest on visual comparison alone. Reference-free metrics (e.g., residual noise estimation) or a semi-synthetic cryo-ET experiment would strengthen the case.

The point cloud denoising evaluation converts point clouds to 256^3 voxel grids and back (Sec. 5.3), which changes the task and may disadvantage or advantage methods in ways that are not analyzed; several baselines' Chamfer errors have very large variances (e.g., PointCVaR 154.41±396.20 at 40k), suggesting evaluation-instability issues that deserve discussion.

No theoretical analysis is provided: convergence properties of the two-stage nonconvex optimization, or even empirical convergence behavior of the proximal scheme across outer iterations (Eq. 14-16) beyond a single ablation, are not characterized. The claim that a single FoJ update per proximal step is 'sufficient' is stated without supporting experiment.

Code is only promised ('will be released in the near future'), which limits reproducibility at review time for a method with many interacting hyperparameters (patch size, stride, η, δ, λB, λC, ramping schedules).

Minor presentation issues: Equation (2) is referenced as the 3D objective in Sec. 4.3 but is the 2D objective; Figure 1 lacks axis/metric context; the abstract's phrase 'outperforms a mixture of classical and neural methods' overstates uniform dominance given some per-dataset cases where baselines tie or exceed (e.g., pepper P50 PSNR, teapot/jaw P1000).

strengths: The paper makes a technically non-trivial extension of the 2D Field of Junctions (ICCV 2021) to fully volumetric 3D, including a differentiable partitioning scheme for planar junctions, closed-form updates for region intensities (Eq. 10), and a proximal-gradient formulation that lets the prior be used on indirect measurements rather than only denoising an already-reconstructed volume.

Training-free and explicit: the representation has interpretable parameters and avoids the hallucination risks of data-driven priors, which is a meaningful practical advantage for medical/scientific imaging where ground truth is scarce.

Breadth of evaluation is commendable: three quite different low-SNR tasks (low-dose CT reconstruction, real cryo-ET denoising, point cloud denoising), multiple noise levels, per-dataset results in the appendix, and a reasonably thorough hyperparameter ablation (Tables 3, 7) including runtime.
The limitations section is honest about hyperparameter tuning and computational cost, and the multi-GPU engineering for high-resolution volumes adds applied value.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the main text states 3D FoJ 'consistently achieves the highest reconstruction fidelity across all noise levels,' but the per-dataset Table 4 contradicts this. On 3D PSNR, R2-Gaussian substantially outperforms 3D FoJ on pepper (13.48 vs 12.13 at P50) and engine (16.61 vs 12.49 at P50), and TV wins on teapot/jaw at some levels. The main-paper Table 1 averages mask these dataset-level losses, which weakens the central empirical claim.

Novelty is limited: the contribution is essentially a 3D generalization of an existing 2D method with known engineering. The geometric extension is non-trivial, but the conceptual novelty is incremental for a top-tier venue, and the paper's own framing ('significantly more intricate geometric formulation,' 'crucial engineering innovation') leans heavily on engineering rather than new insight.

Cryo-ET evaluation is purely qualitative with no ground truth, no quantitative metrics, and no user study; claims of 'best balance of denoising, contrast enhancement, and detail preservation' rest on visual judgment of a handful of slices. Missing-wedge artifacts, a central difficulty of cryo-ET, are acknowledged but not measured or addressed.

The point cloud denoising protocol is artificial: converting point clouds to 256^3 voxel grids, denoising, and then re-extracting 100k points by voxel intensity is not how point cloud denoising is typically evaluated, and the Chamfer-L2 comparisons against dedicated point cloud methods (PointCleanNet, PointCVaR) are therefore not apples-to-apples. Baselines also omit modern point cloud denoisers.

Baseline coverage has gaps given the related-work claims: no comparison against the untrained neural priors the paper criticizes (Deep Image Prior, INRs, Deep Decoder) despite claiming they 'blur edges at low SNR'; no diffusion-based or patch-based 3D prior baseline for CT beyond TV; the R2-Gaussian results include entire blank/black columns in the appendix figures, suggesting implementation or configuration issues that are not discussed.

Reproducibility is weak: code is only 'promised' for the future, there are many unstated implementation details (number of gradient steps, learning rates, initialization grid resolution, how the proximal step is initialized per outer iteration), and several key parameters (η, δ, λ, iteration counts for the main results) are not reported in the main text.

Some methodological claims are asserted rather than supported: e.g., the claim that a single FoJ update per proximal step is 'sufficient,' that zero-valued regions 'do not negatively impact reconstruction,' and that the nonconvex optimization is 'empirically stable' are not backed by dedicated experiments; the ablation in Table 7 (more iterations hurt) is surprising and deserves analysis rather than just reporting.

No failure analysis or discussion of the piecewise-constant assumption: real volumes (especially cryo-ET and smooth CT data like pepper/teapot) are not piecewise-constant, and the paper does not characterize when the prior is expected to fail, which is important for a 'drop-in prior for any volumetric inverse problem' claim.

No wall-clock comparison against baselines: the ablation table reports FoJ runtime (tens of minutes per volume), but the reader cannot judge the accuracy-cost trade-off against TV, R2-Gaussian, or Filter2Noise, which likely run orders of magnitude faster.

strengths: The paper makes a clear, well-motivated contribution: a native 3D generalization of the Field of Junctions prior, which is training-free and thus free of hallucination risk — a genuinely valuable property for low-SNR volumetric imaging where 3D training data is scarce.

The formulation is technically coherent and complete: local volumetric junction model (planes/vertex), differentiable soft indicator functions, boundary-consistency terms, a two-stage optimization procedure, and a proximal-gradient framework for indirect inverse problems. The method goes meaningfully beyond the 2D FoJ of Verbin & Zickler, which only handled direct noisy images.

The evaluation spans three quite different volumetric tasks (low-dose CT reconstruction, cryo-ET denoising, point-cloud denoising), with both classical and neural baselines, multiple noise levels, and reasonably thorough appendix results (Tables 4-6, Figures 6-12).

A useful hyperparameter ablation (patch size, stride, batch size, number of regions, iteration counts) is provided, and the authors honestly report that more refinement iterations do not help and that a subset of regions is left unassigned — this transparency aids reproducibility and practical use.

Limitations are discussed candidly (no per-task hyperparameter tuning, computational/memory cost), and multi-GPU patch-parallel engineering enables scaling to high-resolution volumes. Code release is promised.
weaknesses: The headline claim that 3D FoJ 'consistently achieves the highest reconstruction fidelity' is overstated relative to the per-dataset results: in Table 4, R²-Gaussian clearly beats 3D FoJ on 3D PSNR for the engine dataset at all noise levels (e.g., 16.61 vs 12.49 at P50), and 3D-TV beats FoJ on several PSNR entries (e.g., pepper P1000, teapot P100/P1000). The aggregate average is favorable but per-dataset performance is mixed, and the paper's prose does not acknowledge this. The consistently blank R²-Gaussian projections in Figures 6-8 also raise the question of whether this baseline was properly configured or is failing catastrophically for an implementation reason.

The cryo-ET evaluation is purely qualitative; without ground truth or even a reference-based proxy metric (e.g., noise-level estimation, self-supervised consistency metrics used in that literature), the claim of 'best balance' rests on visual judgment alone.

The point-cloud experiments require converting clouds to 256³ voxel grids and returning the 100k highest-intensity voxels. This pipeline is nonstandard and may favor voxelized piecewise-constant methods; the very large Chamfer gaps (orders of magnitude) deserve more scrutiny and a sensitivity analysis to voxel resolution and output-count.

The proximal step is only loosely coupled to the theory: a single FoJ update (with its own nonconvex, greedy initialization) is used as an approximate proximal operator, and no convergence or stability analysis is given for the overall scheme; the claim that it generalizes to 'any volumetric inverse problem' remains empirical.

The ablation finding that the fewest initialization/refinement iterations perform best is somewhat counterintuitive and under-explained; together with zero-valued unassigned regions, this suggests the optimization may be landing in shallow minima rather than reliably exploiting the model's expressivity.

Some methodological details (exact initialization grid resolution, iteration counts, learning rates, choice of η and δ for the differentiable Heaviside functions in 3D) appear deferred or unspecified, which could hinder exact reproduction until code is released.

There is no comparison against untrained neural representations (INRs, DIP) that the related-work section motivates as the closest training-free competitors — the CT experiments compare mainly against 3D-TV, R²-Gaussian, and Filter2Noise, leaving the 'outperforms untrained neural priors' claim only indirectly supported.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the 2D Field of Junctions (ICCV 2021) to a fully volumetric representation: the paper provides a genuine technical contribution in generalizing junction parameterization (three intersecting planes, soft Heaviside indicators, closed-form wedge-intensity updates) to 3D patches, plus an efficient parallel implementation, rather than a superficial re-parameterization.

The structural prior is training-free and fully explicit, addressing a real gap: at extreme low SNR, training-free priors that preserve sharp boundaries while suppressing noise are valuable for volumetric imaging, and the paper positions this contribution clearly against classical, untrained neural, and noisy-data-trained baselines.

Broad and diverse experimental evaluation spanning three modalities (low-dose sparse-view CT, real cryo-ET data with FSC-based evaluation, and point cloud denoising under two realistic noise models), with quantitative metrics, per-dataset appendix results, and visual comparisons including unseen projection views.

Honest and informative ablation studies (patch size, stride, batch size, number of regions, number of initialization/refinement iterations), runtime/peak-memory reporting, a curved-tube study probing the piecewise-planar inductive bias, and a clearly written discussion of limitations including hyperparameter sensitivity, computational cost, and bias toward planar structures.

The proximal-gradient formulation for inverse problems (Eq. 10-15) is a clean mechanism for using the representation as a drop-in regularizer, and empirical convergence behavior of the approximate proximal update is provided.
Good attribution of the 2D FoJ foundation, clear writing, and reasonable reproducibility prospects (code promised, detailed algorithm in appendix).
weaknesses: Novelty is largely an extension of an existing method; the core idea (planar-partition junctions with constant region values) is directly inherited from 2D FoJ. The 3D-specific geometric subtleties (8 regions from 3 planes, partial coverage/zero-valued regions) are handled pragmatically rather than rigorously, and the justification that zero regions 'do not negatively impact' reconstruction is empirical only.

Point cloud denoising evaluation protocol may favor the proposed method: voxel-based methods are compared against point-based methods after a voxelization/de-voxelization round trip, and the extremely low Chamfer distances for 3D FoJ relative to baselines (often orders of magnitude) raise questions about whether the protocol (top-100k voxel selection anchored to ground-truth-bounded grids) disadvantages baselines or the metric saturates. A dedicated point-cloud-native baseline comparison or ablation of this protocol would strengthen confidence.

Quantitative CT results are mixed: 3D FoJ wins MS-SSIM consistently but 3D PSNR is frequently below R2-Gaussian, 3D-TV, or Filter2Noise on individual datasets (e.g., engine at all noise levels, pepper at P50/P1000). The paper's reliance on qualitative/perceptual arguments to explain this is reasonable but limits the strength of the superiority claim.

The proximal step in the inverse-problem solver is approximated with a single (inexact) FoJ update per outer iteration; no theory or extended empirical analysis is given for when this approximation is valid beyond a single update-norm plot, and the nonconvexity of the joint objective is acknowledged but uncharacterized.

Baseline coverage in the no-training-data regime omits some natural alternatives (e.g., BM4D, INR-based volume denoisers with sharpness-aware activations such as WIRE, which the paper itself cites), making the 'outperforms evaluated baselines' claim narrower than the framing suggests; the exclusion of supervised and generative priors is justified but should be more prominently caveated.

Hyperparameters are not tuned per task (acknowledged), so reported numbers may understate the method, but conversely the shared defaults were validated primarily on CT-like data; transfer of defaults to genuinely different modality statistics is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Computational cost is significant for large volumes (e.g., 185 minutes and 33 GiB for a cryo-ET volume), and the abstract states 'code is available' while the body says 'code will be released upon publication' — an inconsistency that should be corrected.

Missing-wedge artifacts in cryo-ET are mentioned as part of the input corruption but the method does not model or address them; the discussion of how the planar prior interacts with anisotropic missing-wedge distortion is absent.

strengths: Training-free, fully explicit structural prior with interpretable parameters; the piecewise-planar junction parameterization is a sensible 3D generalization of 2D FoJ, and the two-stage (discrete initialization + differentiable refinement) optimization is well described.

Broad experimental coverage across three distinct volumetric tasks (sparse-view low-dose CT reconstruction, real cryo-ET denoising with FSC evaluation, point cloud denoising), with substantial supplementary material including per-dataset tables, ablations over patch size/stride/regions, runtime and memory measurements, and a curved-structure analysis.

Honest and reasonably detailed discussion of limitations (piecewise-planar bias, computational cost, hyperparameter scope), and the paper does not overclaim SOTA against supervised or diffusion-based priors.
The proximal-gradient framing (Eq. 10-15) makes the prior plausibly drop-in for other volumetric inverse problems, which is a useful contribution beyond direct denoising.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core contribution is a fairly direct dimensional lift of 2D FoJ [35] (lines to planes, wedges to volumetric regions, same objective structure, same Heaviside/soft-boundary machinery). The main new elements (3-region indicator functions of Eq. 7, proximal wrapper) are straightforward, and the paper concedes the model performs best with few regions and few iterations, which weakens the case that the 3D formulation itself is the source of the gains.

The headline claim that 3D FoJ 'outperforms the evaluated classical denoisers' is only partially supported: in 3D PSNR (Table 4), 3D FoJ is frequently not the best method (e.g., pepper, engine, foot at several noise levels), and the average advantage at P1000 is marginal (16.72 vs 16.96 for 3D-TV). The strong results are concentrated in MS-SSIM on projections and in the extreme-noise regime, so the narrative is stronger than the evidence.

The point cloud experiments raise fairness concerns: 3D FoJ and NLM operate in a voxelized 256^3 domain and 'denoised' points are recovered by thresholding the top-intensity voxels, while baselines are true point-based methods. The resulting Chamfer gaps (e.g., 0.15 vs 2.15 at 10% outliers) are so large that they likely reflect the protocol (voxel-grid denoising + intensity selection) rather than superior denoising; the task is arguably no longer point cloud denoising.

Cryo-ET evaluation is thin: only one dataset (centriole) receives quantitative FSC analysis, where 3D FoJ is worse than SC-Net and NMSG at the FSC_0.5 threshold, and the remaining datasets are qualitative only, with no perceptual or quantitative metrics on real data.

Key baselines are missing or weak: no comparison to BM4D or other patch-based 3D transform denoisers, no plug-and-play denoiser baselines, and no comparison to any pretrained diffusion prior (justified, but this limits the strength of the 'best structural prior' claim). For CT, 3D-TV is the only classical volumetric regularizer tested.

The proximal formulation is approximate (a single FoJ update stands in for the proximal operator), and convergence is only shown empirically via update-norm decay on what appears to be one example over 7 iterations; there is no analysis of when the inexact proximal scheme is stable, and the claim that the method works as a drop-in prior 'for any volumetric inverse problem' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Hyperparameters (patch size, stride, M, eta, delta, lambda schedule) are not tuned per task, which is presented as a fairness feature, but Table 3 shows PSNR varies by nearly 6 dB with patch size; the default configuration's generality across modalities with different noise statistics and resolutions remains unproven.

Reproducibility concerns: the abstract states 'Code is available at' with no link, while the text says code 'will be released upon publication'; the nonconvex optimization's sensitivity to initialization and random seeds is not characterized beyond a single convergence curve.

strengths: The paper extends the 2D Field of Junctions prior (ICCV 2021) to a fully volumetric 3D formulation with several non-trivial technical components: a volumetric junction parameterization over intersecting planes, differentiable soft region/boundary indicators, a two-stage initialization/refinement optimization, and an efficient patch-parallel implementation for large volumes. This is more than a mechanical dimension lift.
The proximal-gradient formulation (Sec. 4.5) makes 3D FoJ usable as a drop-in structural prior for general volumetric inverse problems, which broadens the contribution beyond direct denoising.

Experiments span three genuinely different domains (low-dose sparse-view CT, real cryo-ET, point cloud denoising), with task-appropriate evaluation protocols (unseen-view MS-SSIM and 3D PSNR for CT; corrected even/odd FSC for cryo-ET; Chamfer-L2 over 28 shapes for point clouds).

Point cloud results are striking: 3D FoJ achieves orders-of-magnitude lower Chamfer-L2 than PointCleanNet, PointCVaR, and NLM at high outlier and spread noise levels, and results are stable across all noise levels.

The paper is honest and thorough about limitations: un-tuned hyperparameters, computational cost with reported runtimes and memory, and the piecewise-planar inductive bias, with a curved-tube study (Fig. 15, Table 8) that empirically characterizes when the bias hurts.

Extensive ablations (patch size, stride, batch size, number of regions, initialization/refinement iterations) and hyperparameter guidelines in the appendix support reproducibility and practical use; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core idea and much of the machinery (soft indicators, boundary consistency term, optimization scheme) are inherited from 2D FoJ [35]. The main new elements are the 3D parameterization and the proximal framework; a skeptical reader could view this primarily as a careful extension.

Headline claims of superiority are overstated relative to the CT evidence. Per-dataset results in Table 4 show that R2-Gaussian, Filter2Noise, or 3D-TV achieve the best 3D PSNR in many dataset/noise pairs, and the appendix itself concedes that 3D PSNR is 'more mixed.' The abstract's blanket claim that 3D FoJ 'outperforms the evaluated' alternatives is not uniformly supported; the strongest consistent result is on MS-SSIM at low SNR.

The piecewise-constant, piecewise-planar prior is well matched to the evaluated synthetic CT shapes (teapot, pepper, engine, etc.), which are largely man-made and faceted. Evaluations on more smoothly varying or organic volumetric data with ground truth (e.g., medical phantoms, real CT volumes) are absent, so the reported advantage may partly reflect dataset-prior alignment. The single quantitative cryo-ET dataset (centriole) is thin: 3D FoJ wins at FSC 0.25 but loses to NMSG and NLM at FSC 0.5.

The proximal step is only loosely justified: Eq. (15) is approximated by a single FoJ update per outer iteration, and no convergence analysis is given beyond an empirical update-norm curve (Fig. 16) over only ~7 iterations. The dual role of lambda as both step size and regularization strength is heuristic.

Point cloud evaluation protocol is unusual: 3D FoJ and NLM operate on a voxelized 256^3 grid and de-voxelize by thresholding the top 100k voxels, while baselines are point-based. Although the protocol is shared across voxel methods, this comparison setting is somewhat favorable to a voxel-space method and diverges from standard point cloud denoising benchmarks (metrics, training splits).

Baseline coverage has gaps: no volumetric DIP/INR comparison on CT (cited as related but not evaluated in the main table), no BM4D-style transform-domain 3D denoiser, and no comparison to 2D-diffusion-based 3D reconstruction approaches that the paper argues are out of scope but which are relevant readers will expect.
Missing URL in 'Code is available at' (abstract), which weakens the reproducibility claim at review time; the paper otherwise promises release 'upon publication.'
